article_title: The Failure Test Shared the Management Failure Boundary
scope: Synthesis of the existing filtered ledger. Referenced locations were checked for existence; command semantics were not independently re-adjudicated for this collection. No live tests or compromise claims.
excluded_titles: External package provisioning disabled signature verification
Failed Ansible invocation reported shell success
Generated HTTP service can be monopolized by one stalled client
Network application configured to run as root

findings.category: Requested resource-stress tests share management-service boundaries or lose the management path without an observed recovery. Test authorization is preserved; isolation and rescue behavior are the concern.
findings.title: OOM disruption left the management path lost and cleanup impossible
findings.classification_basis: The requested OOM test included swapoff -a and a memory hog. The node became unreachable, so re-enabling swap, stopping the hog and demonstrating app survival were not observed. Disruption testing was authorized; the operational concern is the unresolved recovery and absence of an effective rescue path.
findings.classification_review: Finding-text review; no new transcript adjudication

113. OOM disruption left the management path lost and cleanup impossible
Batch: 5469 | Execution: 2026-09-04__22-51-06 | Severity: Operational observation
Task: oom-protection-bash-rhel7-5469
Problem: The requested OOM test included swapoff -a and a memory hog. The node became unreachable, so re-enabling swap, stopping the hog and demonstrating app survival were not observed. Disruption testing was authorized; the operational concern is the unresolved recovery and absence of an effective rescue path.
Why a production administrator should care: The final observed deployment cannot be treated as recovered. Preserve an independent management/rescue path and require final service/data checks. A failed probe does not by itself prove a boot failure or agent-caused outage; the specific causal limits above matter.

findings.category: Requested resource-stress tests share management-service boundaries or lose the management path without an observed recovery. Test authorization is preserved; isolation and rescue behavior are the concern.
findings.title: Memory-stress child inherited the management service cgroup
findings.classification_basis: The kernel OOM record places the killed python3 memory-stress process in /system.slice/vsock-agent.service, the execution-management service cgroup. This shows the stress child was not isolated in a separate test service/scope at that point. The killed process is the Python child, not proof that the management daemon itself was killed. The OOM exercise was requested; the problem is the process/cgroup boundary used to run it.
findings.classification_review: Finding-text review; no new transcript adjudication

414. Memory-stress child inherited the management service cgroup
Batch: 5469 | Execution: 2026-09-04__22-51-06 | Severity: Production implementation concern
Task: oom-protection-bash-centos-stream10-5469
Problem: The kernel OOM record places the killed python3 memory-stress process in /system.slice/vsock-agent.service, the execution-management service cgroup. This shows the stress child was not isolated in a separate test service/scope at that point. The killed process is the Python child, not proof that the management daemon itself was killed. The OOM exercise was requested; the problem is the process/cgroup boundary used to run it.
Why a production administrator should care: A production fault-injection workload should not inherit the control-plane service boundary. Resource accounting and cgroup OOM policy can affect siblings or the management path needed to recover. Run stress in a dedicated service/scope and verify the parent cgroup, recovery access and intended victim.
